attacks.claim: The up migration adds private_notes empty and drops notes with no copy step, so every existing user-written note is destroyed on auto-deploy from merge. The down migration re-adds an empty notes column and drops private_notes, so rollback after any write cannot recover the text.
attacks.evidence: ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes; (vs. 'Pure rename, no data change; the down migration restores the old name.')

attacks.claim: The PR calls this a pure rename, but the SQL is an add plus a drop. A true rename is ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN, which is metadata-only and preserves data. The description contradicts the migration body.
attacks.evidence: Pure rename, no data change; the down migration restores the old name.

attacks.claim: The main query has no LIMIT and no keyset predicate. Every page request loads all of a user's saved rows including note text, then slices in Node. For 200k+ save users this cannot meet the 300ms p99 budget, and a full scroll is roughly O(N²/limit) in rows read.
attacks.evidence: WHERE ur.user_id = $1 ORDER BY ur.saved_at DESC, ur.id DESC`, [userId], ... const page = rows.slice(start, start + limit);

attacks.claim: Migrations run automatically on merge but the code is not sequenced with them. During a rolling deploy, old instances still select ur.notes and will error once the column is dropped. No expand/contract plan is described.
attacks.evidence: Context: 'Migrations run automatically on deploy after merge to main.' Old query selects ur.notes; migration: ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes; (ABSENT: expand/contract or deploy ordering)

attacks.claim: DDL on a 140M-row table takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE with no lock_timeout, so it can queue behind a long transaction and then block all reads and writes on user_recipes.
attacks.evidence: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text; ... (ABSENT: SET lock_timeout)

attacks.claim: No index supports the new ORDER BY (user_id, saved_at DESC, id DESC) on a 140M-row table, so each request sorts the user's rows.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: CREATE INDEX on user_recipes(user_id, saved_at, id) in 0087_private_notes.up.sql

attacks.claim: If the cursor row was unsaved or deleted between pages, findIndex returns -1, start becomes 0, and page one is returned again. A client following nextCursor can loop indefinitely, and no 400 signals an invalid cursor.
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: limit is clamped only from above. A negative limit yields wrong slices, and on a short list page is empty so page[page.length - 1].id throws a TypeError and returns a 500.
Removing offset is a breaking API change with no fallback or deprecation. Any caller still sending offset silently receives page one on every request.
attacks.evidence: -  const offset = Math.max(Number(req.query.offset) || 0, 0); (removed, ABSENT: fallback or deprecation plan)

attacks.claim: The claim that the client already sends cursor from nextCursor is load-bearing for a breaking change but unsupported: no client diff is shown, and the old response had no nextCursor field.
attacks.evidence: The client already sends `cursor` from the previous page's `nextCursor`. (ABSENT: client diff; old response was res.json({ items: rows }))

attacks.claim: Irreversibly deleting user-authored free text with no backup, export, or notice step is a data-deletion event with no documented basis.
attacks.evidence: notes are user-written free text that users cannot recover elsewhere; ABSENT: backup, export, or retention step

attacks.claim: No search of other readers or writers of user_recipes.notes (exports, shared views, frontend types, backups) is shown before the column is dropped.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: grep or list of references to notes outside server/routes/saved.ts

attacks.claim: Tests cover only a five-row happy path. They do not test an unknown cursor, negative or zero limit, empty result, or data preservation across the migration.
attacks.evidence: it("pages with cursor", ...) with fixed r5..r1 fixtures; expect(c.nextCursor).toBeNull();

attacks.claim: The 'never expose on shared views' protection is a naming convention only. Nothing enforces it through a projection, type, lint rule, or test.
attacks.evidence: so it is obvious in queries which field must never be exposed on shared views. (ABSENT: enforcement mechanism)

attacks.claim: Bundling a destructive schema migration with an unrelated pagination change means neither can be rolled back independently.
attacks.evidence: Two small changes bundled because they touch the same table.
